vignette:
Margaret sits in the soft, beige armchair across from me, her hands clasped tightly in her lap. At 73, she carries herself with an air of resilience, yet her eyes often betray a different story—one of fear, sadness, and a long-buried pain that seeps into the fabric of her daily life. The room is quiet, save for the occasional creak of the old wooden house that has held so many of her memories. 

She begins her narrative with hesitation, taking a deep breath as she recalls her childhood. Margaret grew up in a small town in Europe, where her early years were shadowed by the oppressive presence of her mother. “She was strict, but not just strict,” Margaret says, her voice trembling slightly. “It was more like... terror.” 

As she describes the physical punishments, her eyes gloss over, and she visibly flinches at the memories. She talks about the nights she spent curled up in bed, listening to her mother’s footsteps echoing down the hall, the impending dread tightening around her chest. “I’d think, ‘What if she comes for me tonight?’” 

Margaret’s face tightens, and she shakes her head as if to dispel the thoughts she cannot seem to escape. “Even now, sometimes, I hear those footsteps,” she whispers, lowering her gaze to the floor. “It’s like I’m right back there, a little girl again.” 

It is clear that the trauma has woven itself into the very fabric of her existence. As a QA engineer, Margaret has spent her professional life ensuring that software runs smoothly, meticulously checking for flaws. “I think my job is about control,” she explains, her brow furrowing. “If I can catch every bug, then I can prevent something bad from happening.” Yet, the irony of her profession is not lost on her; no amount of quality assurance could have prevented the chaos of her childhood. 

Margaret’s marriage to Tom, a gentle soul who works as a librarian, presents another layer to her story. She describes Tom as her anchor, but even in their loving relationship, shadows of her past loom large. “I can’t let him touch me sometimes,” she confesses, her voice barely a whisper. “I know he loves me, but there are moments when I freeze up, when I just can’t bear the thought of being held.” 

The couple has shared many evenings together, yet Margaret often finds herself retreating into the safety of her own thoughts. During these times, she feels detached, like she is floating above her own life, watching herself move through the motions without truly engaging. “I hate that I do this,” she says, tears brimming in her eyes. “I want to be present, to enjoy our time together, but my mind just... wanders back.” 

She recalls a family gathering last month, when Tom’s sister visited with her children. Margaret had spent the day smiling and engaging, but later that night, as she lay in bed, the laughter of the children felt like a distant echo of her own childhood—the joy laced with an undercurrent of fear. “I had to leave the room,” she admits, her voice breaking. “I just couldn’t handle it.” 

The nightmares have become her constant companions, invading her sleep with vivid images of her mother’s face, twisted in anger, the cracks of her childhood home echoing in her ears. “Every night, it’s the same,” she says, clenching her fists. “I wake up in a cold sweat, heart racing, and my body feels like it’s still back there, like I’m still that scared little girl.” 

Yet, amidst the shadows, there are glimpses of light. Margaret talks about her love for painting, a hobby she took up during her retirement. “It’s the only time I feel free,” she shares, her eyes lighting up momentarily. “When I’m painting, I can pour everything out, all the pain, all the fear—it’s like I’m reclaiming a part of myself.” 

As she continues to navigate the complexities of her past and present, Margaret remains a work in progress. She is learning to find strength in vulnerability, to articulate her fears, and to seek comfort in the love that surrounds her. With every session we share, she takes small, tentative steps toward healing, holding onto the hope that one day, she may finally find peace within herself.
